items.readable_text:
Content:
Previously, we saw that the cardinality of the natural numbers [MATH: \mathbb N] is defined as
[MATH: |\mathbb N| = \aleph_0.]

Content:
Moreover, any countably infinite set also has cardinality [MATH: \aleph_0.] In particular,

Content:
[MATH: |\mathbb Z| = |\mathbb Q| = \aleph_0.]

Content:
This is true because bijections exist between [MATH: \mathbb N] and [MATH: \mathbb Z,] and [MATH: \mathbb N] and [MATH: \mathbb Q.] We've already seen how these bijections are constructed.

Content:
However, not all infinite sets have cardinality [MATH: \aleph_0.] In particular, we have the following important result:

Content:
> The open interval [MATH: (0,1)] of real numbers is uncountable.

Content:
In other words, a bijection does not exist between [MATH: \mathbb N] and [MATH: (0,1).] We can prove this using Cantor's diagonal argument, which we'll discuss later in the lesson.

Content:
The fact that there is no bijection between [MATH: \mathbb N] and [MATH: (0,1)] tells us that although both sets are infinite, the set [MATH: (0,1)] is, in some sense, "bigger" than [MATH: \mathbb N.] We'll make these ideas more precise shortly.

Content:
The cardinality of [MATH: (0,1)] is defined to be [MATH: \mathfrak{c},] which stands for continuum:

Content:
[MATH: \big| (0,1) \big| = \mathfrak{c}]

Content:
Since we're able to construct bijections between other infinite sets and [MATH: (0,1),] we can prove that many sets also have cardinality [MATH: \mathfrak{c}.]

Content:
For example:

Content:
- Since [MATH: f: (0,1) \to \mathbb R] defined by [MATH: f(x) = \cot(\pi x)] is a bijection from [MATH: (0,1)] onto [MATH: \mathbb{R},] we have
[MATH: | \mathbb{R} | = \mathfrak{c}.]
- Since [MATH: f: (0,1) \to \mathbb (a,b)] defined by [MATH: f(x) = a + (b-a)x] is a bijection from [MATH: (0,1)] onto [MATH: (a,b),] we have
[MATH: \big| (a,b) \big| = \mathfrak{c}]
for any [MATH: a < b] and [MATH: a,b \in \mathbb{R}.]

Content:
To summarize,
[MATH: \big| (0,1) \big| = \big| (a,b) \big| = | \mathbb{R} | = \mathfrak{c}.]

Content:
You may wish to make use of these results throughout this lesson.

sections.readable_text:
Consider the following sets.
[MATH: A = \{ x \in \mathbb{R} \mid |x| < 2 \}, \qquad
B= (-3, \infty)]
Which of the following statements are true?

1. [MATH: |A| = \mathfrak{c}]
2. [MATH: |B| = \mathfrak{c}]
3. [MATH: |A| = |B|]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Let's examine our statements in turn.

  • Statement I is true. Solving the restricting inequality for [MATH: x,] we get the following: [MATH: |x||< 2; − 2 < x|< 2] As a result, [MATH: A = (-2, 2).] Notice that the function [MATH: x \to 4x-2] is a bijection that maps [MATH: (0,1)] onto [MATH: (-2,2).] So, [MATH: |A| = |(0,1)| = \mathfrak{c}.]

  • Statement II is true. The function [MATH: x \to e^x-3] is a bijection that maps [MATH: (-\infty, \infty)=\mathbb{R}] onto [MATH: (-3, \infty).] So, [MATH: |B| = |\mathbb{R}| = \mathfrak{c}.]

  • Statement III is true. Indeed, we have [MATH: |A| = \mathfrak{c} = |B|.]

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."

items.readable_text:
Content:
Let's now prove the theorem stated earlier:

Content:
> The open interval [MATH: (0,1)] of real numbers is uncountable.

Content:
We'll prove this by showing that a contradiction arises by assuming [MATH: (0,1)] is countably infinite.

Content:
So, suppose there exists a bijection [MATH: f: \mathbb{N} \to (0,1)] such that all the elements of [MATH: (0,1)] can be listed in a sequence, as shown below.

Content:
| [MATH: \mathbb{N}] | | [MATH: (0,1)] |
| [MATH: 1] | [MATH: \overset{f}{\longleftrightarrow}] | [MATH: 0 \: . \: \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}a_{11}} \: a_{12} \: a_{13} \: \ldots \: a_{1n} \: \ldots] |
| [MATH: 2] | [MATH: \overset{f}{\longleftrightarrow}] | [MATH: 0 \: . \: a_{21} \: \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}a_{22}} \: a_{23} \: \ldots \: a_{2n} \: \ldots] |
| [MATH: 3] | [MATH: \overset{f}{\longleftrightarrow}] | [MATH: 0 \: . \: a_{31} \: a_{32} \: \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}a_{33}} \: \ldots \: a_{3n} \: \ldots] |
| [MATH: \vdots] | | [MATH: \vdots] |
| [MATH: n] | [MATH: \overset{f}{\longleftrightarrow}] | [MATH: 0 \: . \: a_{n1} \: a_{n2} \: a_{n3} \: \ldots \: \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}a_{nn}} \: \ldots] |
| [MATH: \vdots] | | [MATH: \vdots] |

Content:
Note that [MATH: a_{ij}] denotes the digit in the [MATH: j]th decimal place for the [MATH: i]th number in our list.

Content:
Now, let's show that there is a number in [MATH: (0,1)] that does not belong to this list. To do that, we consider the digits after the decimal point that lie on the "diagonal" of our list (denoted [MATH: \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}a_{ii}}] for [MATH: i=1,2,3,\ldots).]

Content:
We define a new number [MATH: b = 0 . b_1 b_2 \ldots b_n \ldots] whose digits are selected from [MATH: \{ 1, 2 \}] such that

Content:
[MATH: {2,|ifa_{ii} = 1; 1,|ifa_{ii} ≠ 1.]

Content:
Now, notice that

Content:
- [MATH: b] can't be the [MATH: 1]st number on the list since [MATH: b_1 \neq a_{11},]
- [MATH: b] can't be the [MATH: 2]nd number on the list since [MATH: b_2 \neq a_{22},]
- [MATH: b] can't be the [MATH: 3]rd number on the list since [MATH: b_3 \neq a_{33},]
- [MATH: \cdots]

Content:
and so on. As a result, [MATH: b] is not on the list, which is a contradiction! Hence, the assumption that there exists a bijection [MATH: f: \mathbb{N} \to (0,1)] is false!

Content:
Therefore, we conclude that no bijection maps [MATH: \mathbb N] onto [MATH: (0,1),] and so [MATH: (0,1)] is uncountable.

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Previously, we saw that the cardinality of the natural numbers [MATH: \mathbb N] is defined as
[MATH: |\mathbb N| = \aleph_0.]

Content:
Moreover, any countably infinite set also has cardinality [MATH: \aleph_0.] In particular,

Content:
[MATH: |\mathbb Z| = |\mathbb Q| = \aleph_0.]

Content:
This is true because bijections exist between [MATH: \mathbb N] and [MATH: \mathbb Z,] and [MATH: \mathbb N] and [MATH: \mathbb Q.] We've already seen how these bijections are constructed.

Content:
However, not all infinite sets have cardinality [MATH: \aleph_0.] In particular, we have the following important result:

Content:
> The open interval [MATH: (0,1)] of real numbers is uncountable.

Content:
In other words, a bijection does not exist between [MATH: \mathbb N] and [MATH: (0,1).] We can prove this using Cantor's diagonal argument, which we'll discuss later in the lesson.

Content:
The fact that there is no bijection between [MATH: \mathbb N] and [MATH: (0,1)] tells us that although both sets are infinite, the set [MATH: (0,1)] is, in some sense, "bigger" than [MATH: \mathbb N.] We'll make these ideas more precise shortly.

Content:
The cardinality of [MATH: (0,1)] is defined to be [MATH: \mathfrak{c},] which stands for continuum:

Content:
[MATH: \big| (0,1) \big| = \mathfrak{c}]

Content:
Since we're able to construct bijections between other infinite sets and [MATH: (0,1),] we can prove that many sets also have cardinality [MATH: \mathfrak{c}.]

Content:
For example:

Content:
- Since [MATH: f: (0,1) \to \mathbb R] defined by [MATH: f(x) = \cot(\pi x)] is a bijection from [MATH: (0,1)] onto [MATH: \mathbb{R},] we have
[MATH: | \mathbb{R} | = \mathfrak{c}.]
- Since [MATH: f: (0,1) \to \mathbb (a,b)] defined by [MATH: f(x) = a + (b-a)x] is a bijection from [MATH: (0,1)] onto [MATH: (a,b),] we have
[MATH: \big| (a,b) \big| = \mathfrak{c}]
for any [MATH: a < b] and [MATH: a,b \in \mathbb{R}.]

Content:
To summarize,
[MATH: \big| (0,1) \big| = \big| (a,b) \big| = | \mathbb{R} | = \mathfrak{c}.]

Content:
You may wish to make use of these results throughout this lesson.

---

Item 2 — Example: Identifying Sets of Cardinality Continuum

Example Prompt:
Consider the following sets.
[MATH: A = \{ x \in \mathbb{R} \mid |x| < 2 \}, \qquad
B= (-3, \infty)]
Which of the following statements are true?

1. [MATH: |A| = \mathfrak{c}]
2. [MATH: |B| = \mathfrak{c}]
3. [MATH: |A| = |B|]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Solving the restricting inequality for [MATH: x,] we get the following:
[MATH: |x||< 2; − 2 < x|< 2]
As a result, [MATH: A = (-2, 2).] Notice that the function [MATH: x \to 4x-2] is a bijection that maps [MATH: (0,1)] onto [MATH: (-2,2).] So,
[MATH: |A| = |(0,1)| = \mathfrak{c}.]
- Statement II is true. The function [MATH: x \to e^x-3] is a bijection that maps [MATH: (-\infty, \infty)=\mathbb{R}] onto [MATH: (-3, \infty).] So,
[MATH: |B| = |\mathbb{R}| = \mathfrak{c}.]
- Statement III is true. Indeed, we have
[MATH: |A| = \mathfrak{c} = |B|.]

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."

---

Item 5 — Tutorial: Cantor's Diagonal Argument

Content:
Let's now prove the theorem stated earlier:

Content:
> The open interval [MATH: (0,1)] of real numbers is uncountable.

Content:
We'll prove this by showing that a contradiction arises by assuming [MATH: (0,1)] is countably infinite.

Content:
So, suppose there exists a bijection [MATH: f: \mathbb{N} \to (0,1)] such that all the elements of [MATH: (0,1)] can be listed in a sequence, as shown below.

Content:
| [MATH: \mathbb{N}] | | [MATH: (0,1)] |
| [MATH: 1] | [MATH: \overset{f}{\longleftrightarrow}] | [MATH: 0 \: . \: \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}a_{11}} \: a_{12} \: a_{13} \: \ldots \: a_{1n} \: \ldots] |
| [MATH: 2] | [MATH: \overset{f}{\longleftrightarrow}] | [MATH: 0 \: . \: a_{21} \: \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}a_{22}} \: a_{23} \: \ldots \: a_{2n} \: \ldots] |
| [MATH: 3] | [MATH: \overset{f}{\longleftrightarrow}] | [MATH: 0 \: . \: a_{31} \: a_{32} \: \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}a_{33}} \: \ldots \: a_{3n} \: \ldots] |
| [MATH: \vdots] | | [MATH: \vdots] |
| [MATH: n] | [MATH: \overset{f}{\longleftrightarrow}] | [MATH: 0 \: . \: a_{n1} \: a_{n2} \: a_{n3} \: \ldots \: \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}a_{nn}} \: \ldots] |
| [MATH: \vdots] | | [MATH: \vdots] |

Content:
Note that [MATH: a_{ij}] denotes the digit in the [MATH: j]th decimal place for the [MATH: i]th number in our list.

Content:
Now, let's show that there is a number in [MATH: (0,1)] that does not belong to this list. To do that, we consider the digits after the decimal point that lie on the "diagonal" of our list (denoted [MATH: \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}a_{ii}}] for [MATH: i=1,2,3,\ldots).]

Content:
We define a new number [MATH: b = 0 . b_1 b_2 \ldots b_n \ldots] whose digits are selected from [MATH: \{ 1, 2 \}] such that

Content:
[MATH: {2,|ifa_{ii} = 1; 1,|ifa_{ii} ≠ 1.]

Content:
Now, notice that

Content:
- [MATH: b] can't be the [MATH: 1]st number on the list since [MATH: b_1 \neq a_{11},]
- [MATH: b] can't be the [MATH: 2]nd number on the list since [MATH: b_2 \neq a_{22},]
- [MATH: b] can't be the [MATH: 3]rd number on the list since [MATH: b_3 \neq a_{33},]
- [MATH: \cdots]

Content:
and so on. As a result, [MATH: b] is not on the list, which is a contradiction! Hence, the assumption that there exists a bijection [MATH: f: \mathbb{N} \to (0,1)] is false!

Content:
Therefore, we conclude that no bijection maps [MATH: \mathbb N] onto [MATH: (0,1),] and so [MATH: (0,1)] is uncountable.

---
